entries.notes: Verb stem + 고 싶다. For someone else, use -고 싶어 하다.

examples.en: I want to drink coffee.
I want to go to Korea.
Today I want to rest at home.

entries.notes: Stem with ㅏ/ㅗ → 아요, other vowels → 어요, 하다 → 해요.

examples.en: I go to school.
I eat a meal.
I study Korean every day.

entries.notes: Stem with ㅏ/ㅗ → 았어요, other vowels → 었어요, 하다 → 했어요.

examples.en: I met a friend yesterday.
I already ate lunch.
I watched a movie at the weekend.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄹ 거예요, consonant stem → 을 거예요.

examples.en: It will rain tomorrow.
I'm going to Busan next week.
I'm going to read a book this evening.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 고 있다.

examples.en: I'm listening to music now.
My younger sibling is sleeping.
I'm learning the guitar these days.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄹ 수 있다, consonant stem → 을 수 있다.

examples.en: I can read Hangul.
Can you come tomorrow?
You can take photos here.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄹ 수 없다, consonant stem → 을 수 없다.

examples.en: I can't meet today.
It's too spicy, so I can't eat it.
I can't find the password.

entries.notes: 아/어 form of the verb + 주세요.

examples.en: Please speak slowly.
Please open the door.
Please take a photo for me.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → 세요, consonant stem → 으세요.

examples.en: Please sit here.
Goodbye. (Go in peace.)
Please wash your hands.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 지 마세요.

examples.en: Don't worry.
Please don't smoke here.
Please don't be late.

entries.notes: 아/어 form + 야 하다 (or 돼 in speech: 해야 돼요).

examples.en: I have to get up early tomorrow.
I have to do my homework.
You have to take the medicine.

entries.notes: Stem + 고 links two actions or states.

examples.en: I ate and then drank coffee.
This restaurant is cheap and tasty.
My older brother is tall and my younger one is short.

entries.notes: Stem + 지만.

examples.en: Korean is hard but fun.
It was expensive, but I bought it.
I'm tired, but I'm going to work out.

entries.notes: 아/어 form + 서. Never with past tense or commands.

examples.en: I was hungry, so I ate ramyeon.
Sorry for being late.
I met a friend and we watched a movie together.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → 니까, consonant stem → 으니까. Works with commands and suggestions.

examples.en: It's raining, so take an umbrella.
We have no time, so let's hurry.
It's cold, so I'll close the window.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → 면, consonant stem → 으면.

examples.en: If you have time, let's go together.
If you're tired, rest a bit.
When spring comes, flowers bloom.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 기 전에.

examples.en: I brush my teeth before bed.
Wash your hands before eating.
I'll call before I leave.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄴ 후에, consonant stem → 은 후에.

examples.en: Let's meet after class.
I took a walk after eating.
After graduating, I joined a company.

entries.notes: Vowel or ㄹ stem → 러, consonant stem → 으러; then 가다/오다.

examples.en: Let's go and eat.
I'm going to a café to meet a friend.
I went to the library to borrow a book.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄹ까요, consonant stem → 을까요.

examples.en: Shall we have lunch together?
Shall I open the window?
I wonder if the weather will be nice tomorrow.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㅂ시다, consonant stem → 읍시다. Avoid with seniors.

examples.en: Let's go together.
Let's rest here for a moment.
Let's begin now.

entries.notes: 아/어 form + 보다.

examples.en: Try these clothes on.
I've tried kimchi.
I'll give it a try.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄴ 적이 있다, consonant stem → 은 적이 있다. Never: 없다.

examples.en: I have been to Korea.
Have you seen that movie?
I've never skied.

entries.notes: Stem + 네요 (ㄹ drops: 머네요). Fresh surprise or admiration.

examples.en: The weather is really nice!
You speak Korean well!
Oh, it's already ten o'clock.

entries.notes: Stem + 죠 (short for 지요). Seeks agreement or softly suggests.

examples.en: This is tasty, right?
You have time tomorrow, right?
Let's go together.

entries.notes: Verbs and 있다/없다 → 는데; adjectives → (으)ㄴ데; nouns → 인데.

examples.en: It's raining, but I don't have an umbrella.
I'm hungry. Shall we go and eat?
This bag is pretty but too expensive.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄹ게요, consonant stem → 을게요. First person only.

examples.en: I'll do it.
I'll call you later.
I'll wait here.

entries.notes: Stem + 겠다.

examples.en: That looks tasty!
I will come again tomorrow.
You must be very tired.

entries.notes: Stem + 기 때문에; nouns take 때문에 directly.

examples.en: The game was cancelled because of the rain.
I have an exam, so I have to study.
I can't go because I'm busy.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 고 싶어 하다, for a third person.

examples.en: My younger sibling wants to raise a puppy.
My friend wants to go to Korea.
The kids want to play.

entries.notes: Vowel or ㄹ stem → 려고, consonant stem → 으려고.

examples.en: I'm planning to move next year.
I intend to go hiking this weekend.
I was just about to go out.

entries.notes: 아/어 form + 도 되다.

examples.en: May I sit here?
You may take photos.
Would it be okay to open the window?

entries.notes: Vowel stem → 면, consonant stem → 으면, then 안 되다.

examples.en: You must not swim here.
You must not sleep in class.
You mustn't be late.

entries.notes: Stem + 지 않다. Short form: 안 + verb.

examples.en: It's not cold today.
I don't eat meat.
That movie wasn't fun.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 지 못하다. Short form: 못 + verb.

examples.en: I couldn't sleep last night.
I couldn't finish my homework.
I can't swim.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 는 것 (spoken: 는 거).

examples.en: I like singing.
Cooking is fun.
Learning Korean isn't easy.

entries.notes: Stem + 기. Common with 좋다, 싫다, 어렵다, 쉽다.

examples.en: My hobby is taking photos.
In Korean, speaking is hard.
Getting up early is hard.

entries.notes: Present verb → 는 것 같다; adjective or past verb → (으)ㄴ 것 같다.

examples.en: It seems to be raining outside.

examples.ko: 이 옷이 좀 큰 것 같아요.
examples.en: I think these clothes are a bit big.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 벌써 간 것 같아요.
examples.en: I think that person has already left.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄹ 것 같다, consonant stem → 을 것 같다.

examples.en: It looks like it'll rain soon.
I think I'll be late today.
This movie looks like it'll be fun.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 게 되다. A change not fully your own choice.

examples.ko: 그 노래 때문에 한국어를 공부하게 됐어요.
examples.en: That song got me studying Korean.
It turns out I'm moving to Seoul next month.
Thanks to a friend, I started eating kimchi.

entries.notes: Adjective 아/어 form + 지다.

examples.en: The weather has got warm.
Korean is getting easier and easier.
The room has become clean.

entries.notes: Adjective stem + 게 turns it into an adverb.

examples.en: Enjoy your meal.
Please speak up.
I cleaned the room thoroughly.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 는 동안; nouns take 동안 directly.

examples.en: Please wait while I cook.
I learned a lot while living in Korea.
I cleaned while the baby was sleeping.

entries.notes: Vowel or ㄹ stem → 면서, consonant stem → 으면서. Same subject.

examples.en: I study while listening to music.
We talked while eating.
Don't talk on the phone while walking.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄹ 때, consonant stem → 을 때.

examples.en: I lived in Busan when I was young.
Get in touch when you have time.
I drink coffee when I'm tired.

entries.notes: Stem + 거나; nouns take (이)나.

examples.en: At weekends I read or watch movies.
I take the bus or walk.
If you have a question or don't understand, ask.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 고 나서.

examples.en: I play after doing my homework.
I went to sleep after showering.
After the movie, we had dinner.

entries.notes: Intransitive or passive verb 아/어 form + 있다 (a result that lasts).

examples.en: The door is open.
I'm sitting on the chair.
There are flowers on the desk.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 기로 하다.

examples.en: We decided to meet tomorrow.
I've decided to exercise this year.
I decided to quit smoking.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄹ래요, consonant stem → 을래요. Casual intention.

examples.en: What would you like to drink?
I'll have bibimbap.
Do you want to walk together?

entries.notes: Stem + 잖아요; nouns take (이)잖아요.

examples.en: I told you, didn't I?
It's Sunday today, you know.
It's cold outside, you know.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄹ 줄 알다, consonant stem → 을 줄 알다.

examples.en: I know how to drive.
Do you know how to make kimchi stew?
I know how to play the guitar.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄹ 줄 모르다, consonant stem → 을 줄 모르다.

examples.en: I don't know how to swim.
I can't read Chinese characters.
I don't know how to ride a bike.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 기 시작하다.

examples.en: It started to rain.
I started learning Korean last year.
The baby started walking.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 는 게 좋다 (게 = 것이). 좋겠어요 is softer.

examples.en: It's better to go to bed early.
You'd better take a taxi.
It's good to drink plenty of water.

entries.notes: 아/어 form + 버리다. Completion, often with relief or regret.

examples.en: I ate up all the cake.
The bus has already left.
My friend went on ahead without me.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄹ 필요가 없다, consonant stem → 을 필요가 없다.

examples.en: There's no need to worry.
You don't need to come early.
There's no need to book.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄴ 지, consonant stem → 은 지, then a time + 되다/지나다.

examples.ko: 한국어를 배운 지 일 년이 됐어요.
examples.en: It's been a year since I started learning Korean.

examples.ko: 서울에 산 지 오 년이 됐어요.
examples.en: I've lived in Seoul for five years.

examples.ko: 밥을 먹은 지 한 시간 됐어요.
examples.en: It's been an hour since I ate.

entries.notes: Noun + 보다, often with 더 (more).

examples.en: Today is colder than yesterday.
I like tea more than coffee.
The train is faster than the bus.

entries.notes: Noun + 처럼.

examples.en: You sing as well as a singer.
I was happy, like in a dream.
I laughed like a child.

entries.notes: Noun + 만.

examples.en: I only drink water.
I came early just today.
Please say it just once more.

entries.notes: Noun + 도 (replaces 은/는, 이/가, 을/를).

examples.en: I'm a student too.
I eat both meat and fish.
It's raining tomorrow too.

entries.notes: Noun + 밖에 + a negative (없다, 안, 못).

examples.en: I only have a thousand won in my wallet.
We only have ten minutes.
Is this all there is?

entries.notes: Time + 부터 … time + 까지. For places: 에서 … 까지.

examples.en: I work from nine to six.
I have classes from Monday to Friday.
I read it from beginning to end.

entries.notes: Person + 에게 (written) or 한테 (spoken); honorific: 께.

examples.en: I gave a present to a friend.
I wrote a letter to Mum.
Ask the teacher.

entries.notes: Vowel noun → 나, consonant noun → 이나.

examples.en: Would you like coffee or tea?
Shall we watch a movie or something this weekend?
I ate as many as five apples.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 나요? A gentle, polite question.

examples.en: Does this bus go to City Hall?
When do you arrive?
Are you open tomorrow too?

entries.notes: Adjective stem + 군요; verb stem + 는군요; noun + (이)군요.

examples.en: Ah, I see.
There are a lot of people today, I see.
You really do speak Korean well.

entries.notes: Stem + 거든요. Gives the reason or background after the fact.

examples.en: I can't go today. I have plans, you see.
I'm full. I ate a lot earlier, you see.
I like that song. The lyrics are pretty, you see.

entries.notes: Adjective + 다고; verb + (느)ㄴ다고; noun + (이)라고 하다.

examples.en: My friend said they'd come tomorrow.
They say it'll rain tomorrow.
They say that restaurant is good.

entries.notes: Vowel or ㄹ stem → 라고, consonant stem → 으라고 하다. Reports a command.

examples.en: Mum told me to go to bed early.
The teacher told us to read the book.
The doctor told me to get plenty of rest.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 는 중이다; nouns take 중이다.

examples.en: I'm in a meeting right now.
I'm on my way home.
I'm in the middle of eating.

entries.notes: Verb → 는 편이다; adjective → (으)ㄴ 편이다.

examples.ko: 저는 매운 음식을 잘 먹는 편이에요.
examples.en: I tend to handle spicy food well.
This neighbourhood is fairly quiet.
My older brother is on the tall side.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 기 쉽다.

examples.en: This book is easy to read.
It's easy to catch a cold in winter.
This word is easy to memorise.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 기 어렵다.

examples.en: This problem is hard to solve.
Korean pronunciation is hard to imitate.
It's hard to get up in the morning.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄹ 뻔하다, consonant stem → 을 뻔하다. Usually past: 뻔했어요.

examples.en: I almost missed the bus.
I nearly fell over.
I almost forgot the appointment.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄹ수록, consonant stem → 을수록. Often -(으)면 -(으)ㄹ수록.

examples.en: The more you practise, the better you get.
The more I see it, the more I like it.
The more people, the more fun.

entries.notes: 아/어 form + 도. Often with 아무리 (however).

examples.en: I'll go even if it rains.
However busy you are, you have to eat.
It's fine even if you're late.

entries.notes: Verb stem + 도록. Purpose or degree.

examples.en: I took a note so I wouldn't forget.
Leave early so you won't be late.
Take care not to catch a cold.

entries.notes: Past stem (았/었) + 으면 좋겠다.

examples.en: I hope the weather is nice tomorrow.
I wish the holidays would come soon.
I hope I passed the exam.

entries.notes: Verb → 는 대신에; nouns take 대신에 directly.

examples.en: I drink tea instead of coffee.
Instead of taking a taxi, I walked.
I rest today and work tomorrow instead.

entries.notes: Verb → (으)ㄴ/는 김에. Doing one thing as a chance to do another.

examples.en: While I was at the market, I bought fruit too.
Since it's come up, let me ask you something.
While you're up, could you get me some water?

entries.notes: Verb stem + 다가. An action is interrupted or changes.

examples.en: On my way home, I ran into a friend.
I fell asleep while studying.
I fell while walking.

entries.notes: Vowel stem → ㄹ 테니까, consonant stem → 을 테니까. My intention as a reason.

examples.en: I'll drive, so get some rest.
We'll arrive soon, so wait just a little.
I'll explain, so listen carefully.

entries.notes: 아/어 form + 놓다 (or 두다). The result is kept for later.

examples.en: I bought the tickets in advance.
Please leave the window open.
I'll have the food ready.

entries.notes: Verb → 는 줄 알았다; adjective or past verb → (으)ㄴ 줄 알았다.

examples.en: I thought today was Saturday.
I thought you'd already left.
I thought you were Korean.

entries.notes: Stem + 지요. Formal-sounding version of -죠.

examples.en: This is the right way, isn't it?
It's really hot, isn't it?
Everyone is here, right?
